phase1.explanation:
Okay, first things first — what even IS Java?

Think of it like this: I'm basically running a workshop where I build things, and every single tool and blueprint I use is written in Java. James Gosling and his team built the language back in 1995 at Sun Microsystems, and the one rule they cared about most was: whatever you build here should work everywhere, not just on the one machine you built it on.

That rule has a name — [[term:WORA]], Write Once, Run Anywhere. Here's how it actually works: you write your code, and instead of turning it directly into instructions for YOUR specific computer, it gets compiled into something called [[term:bytecode]] — a kind of universal blueprint. Then any machine with a [[term:JVM]] (Java Virtual Machine) installed can read that blueprint and run it, whether it's Windows, Mac, Linux, or — I promise I'm not exaggerating — an actual internet-connected fridge somewhere.

A few things about how I like to build with Java, since these will come up constantly:

I build with [[key:objects, not just instructions]]. Almost everything you'll write with me is a blueprint (we call it a [[term:class]]) for some kind of object — a BankAccount, a Shape, a Person. You design the blueprint once, then make as many objects from it as you want.

I label everything before I use it. Java is [[term:strongly typed]] — it wants to know a variable's type up front, before you're allowed to use it. [[warn:Feels strict at first]]. It's actually just Java double-checking your work before you get too far in.

I don't clean up after myself, and neither do you — the JVM does. Java has [[term:garbage collection]], which means once you're done with something, you can just stop using it, and the JVM quietly clears it out of memory for you.

And that WORA thing I mentioned? That's the [[term:platform independence]] part — the JVM is what makes it possible.

We're following the CS22301 syllabus together, so we're doing this in order: OOP ideas first — the blueprints-and-objects way of thinking — and then we'll go deeper into how Java actually pulls it off under the hood.

mcq.question:
Quick check before we start building — which of these is actually true about Java?

A) Your compiled program only runs on the machine that compiled it
B) Java uses raw pointers like C or C++
C) Write Once, Run Anywhere — the same bytecode runs on any machine with a JVM
D) You have to manually free memory yourself

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: Java wasn't always called Java! Gosling's team first called the project "Oak," after a tree outside his office. When it turned out another company already had "Oak" trademarked, the team went looking for a new name during a coffee run — and "Java," slang for coffee, stuck. That's also why the logo is a steaming coffee cup. Every time you see that cup icon, that's a coffee run that changed programming history.
phase5.openingDialogue: Before you go — one more thing I think you'll like~
